column1: # Columns are TAB separated. Lines starting with # are ignored.
# Add your own rows here, or (better) in ~/.config/silverdetector/data/ports.tsv -
# a row there replaces the row with the same port number, so you can disagree with
# anything below without editing this file.
# risk   normal        expected anywhere, exposed or not              -> OK
#        local         fine on 127.0.0.1, wrong when it answers off-box -> OK / WARN
#        local-strict  same, but unauthenticated by default            -> OK / CRIT
#        sensitive     worth a look wherever it is                     -> NOTICE / WARN
#        dangerous     cleartext, legacy or routinely exploited        -> WARN / CRIT
#        malware       default port of a handler, backdoor or C2       -> CRIT always

column5: description
Echo service. Obsolete, and a UDP amplification reflector. Nothing should run this.
Discard service (/dev/null over the network). Occasionally used by Wake-on-LAN tooling.
Daytime. Obsolete diagnostic service, usable for amplification.
Quote of the day. Obsolete, amplification reflector.
Character generator. Classic UDP amplification source, disable it.
FTP data channel. Cleartext file transfer.
FTP control channel. Credentials and data travel in cleartext; check for anonymous login.
OpenSSH. Encrypted remote login and file transfer. Expected on almost every Linux box.
Telnet. Login and session in cleartext on the wire. Should not be running in 2020s.
Mail submission/relay. Check it is not an open relay if it answers off-box.
Time protocol. Obsolete, amplification reflector.
WHOIS server. Unusual on a workstation.
TACACS+ device authentication. Network-gear infrastructure, not a laptop service.
DNS. On a desktop this is normally systemd-resolved or dnsmasq on 127.0.0.53. Answering off-box makes you an open resolver.
DHCP server. Normal on a router or when you are running a rogue-DHCP test; not on a plain client.
DHCP client. Every machine that gets an address by DHCP has this.
TFTP. No authentication at all; frequently holds router configs and PXE images.
Finger. Leaks usernames and login times. Obsolete.
Plain HTTP web server. Normal, but anything it serves is unencrypted.
Kerberos KDC. Means this host is a domain controller or a KDC.
POP3 mail retrieval in cleartext. Use 995 instead.
RPC portmapper. Enumerates every RPC service on the host; a classic recon target when exposed.
Ident. Leaks the local username behind a connection.
Usenet news transport. Very unusual on a modern host.
NTP time sync. Normal; only worth a look if it answers queries from the network (monlist amplification).
Microsoft RPC endpoint mapper. A Windows host, and a prime enumeration/exploitation target.
NetBIOS name service. Leaks host and domain names; poisonable (Responder).
NetBIOS datagram service. Legacy Windows file sharing.
NetBIOS session service (SMB over NetBIOS). Legacy SMB, should be off in favour of 445.
IMAP mail access. Cleartext unless STARTTLS is enforced; prefer 993.
SNMP. Community strings are often left as public/private and give full device inventory.
SNMP trap receiver. Monitoring infrastructure.
X Display Manager Control Protocol. Remote X login with weak authentication.
BGP routing daemon. Router infrastructure.
LDAP directory. Cleartext unless STARTTLS; often allows anonymous bind and full directory dumps.
Service Location Protocol. Amplification reflector, and leaks the service inventory.
TLS web server. Normal on anything serving web content.
SMB file sharing. The single most attacked port on Windows networks; check signing and shares.
Kerberos password change service. Goes with a KDC.
SMTP over implicit TLS. Normal mail submission.
IPsec IKE. A VPN endpoint; aggressive mode can leak PSK hashes.
Modbus TCP. Industrial control protocol with no authentication whatsoever.
rexec. Cleartext remote execution, obsolete r-service.
rlogin. Trust-based remote login, obsolete r-service.
rsh. Trust-based remote shell, obsolete r-service.
Syslog receiver. Fine on a log server; on a workstation it means you are collecting someone's logs.
LPD print service. Legacy printing, has a history of remote code execution bugs.
RIP routing. Unauthenticated route injection.
IBM DB2 discovery service.
UUCP. Obsolete.
Apple Filing Protocol. macOS file sharing.
RTSP streaming. Usually a camera or media server; often has no authentication.
SMTP mail submission with STARTTLS. Normal for a mail client or relay.
RPC over HTTP endpoint mapper. Windows infrastructure.
IPMI/BMC (iDRAC, iLO). Out-of-band server management with a long history of authentication bypasses.
CUPS printing. Normal bound to localhost; exposed it advertises your printers and has had RCE bugs.
LDAP over TLS. Directory service, encrypted. On a domain controller, the relay target for LDAP(S) attacks (RBCD, Shadow Credentials) when channel binding is off.
Active Directory global catalog over TLS. This host is a domain controller.
Active Directory Web Services (ADWS). Backs the PowerShell AD module and SOAPHound-style enumeration; its presence confirms a domain controller.
MPLS label distribution. Router infrastructure.
Rarely legitimate. Sometimes used by backdoors.
Industrial HMI protocol.
rsync daemon. Often exposes whole trees with no authentication; check the modules.
VMware authentication daemon. Hypervisor management.
IMAP over TLS. Normal mail access.
POP3 over TLS. Normal mail access.
SOCKS proxy. Expected if you started proxychains/ssh -D yourself; otherwise it is an open pivot.
Java RMI registry. Deserialisation RCE is close to automatic here.
OpenVPN endpoint. Fine if you run a VPN, notable otherwise.
No standard service. Common for VLC streams and, just as often, hand-rolled netcat listeners.
No legitimate registration. Overwhelmingly a hand-placed backdoor or a CTF service.
Microsoft SQL Server. Should never face the network directly.
MSSQL browser service. Leaks instance names, amplification reflector.
Oracle TNS listener. Enumerable SIDs, historically weak defaults.
PPTP VPN. MS-CHAPv2 is broken; treat any credential used here as compromised.
MQTT broker. Frequently unauthenticated and world-readable.
UPnP discovery. Leaks device inventory, strong amplification reflector.
IANA registers this to Cisco SCCP ("Skinny") VoIP call control. In practice it is just as often an ad-hoc application or dev server, so identify the owning process before calling it normal.
Cisco SCCP ("Skinny") VoIP signalling.
NFS. no_root_squash and world-readable exports are a standard route to root.
cPanel control panel (plain).
cPanel control panel (TLS).
FTP on an alternate port. Same cleartext problem as 21.
Apache ZooKeeper. Unauthenticated by default; exposed it hands over cluster configuration.
SSH on a non-standard port. Normal if you moved it deliberately; otherwise find out who started it.
Docker daemon API without TLS. Anyone who reaches it is root on the host - it is a root shell as a service.
Docker daemon API with TLS. Still full host control for whoever holds a client certificate.
etcd client API. Holds Kubernetes secrets in the clear if unauthenticated.
etcd peer traffic.
Oracle TNS (unencrypted alternate).
Common development server port (Node, Rails, Grafana). Fine on localhost; exposed it is usually an accident.
Squid HTTP proxy. An open proxy lets anyone browse from your IP.
iSCSI target. Raw block-device access over the network.
Active Directory global catalog. This host is a domain controller.
MySQL/MariaDB. Normal on loopback for a local app; database ports should not face the network.
Windows Remote Desktop. High-value target; check NLA is required.
distcc daemon. Remote command execution by design (CVE-2004-2687).
IANA registers 4000 to Terabase, but in the field it is almost always an application or dev server (and 4000/udp was ICQ). Nothing standard on a Linux box listens here - identify the process.
Historically ICQ. Nothing standard listens here today.
Spark/dev tooling web UI. Also ngrok's local inspector.
Erlang port mapper (RabbitMQ, CouchDB). Leaks node names; with a guessable cookie it is remote code execution.
Metasploit's default handler/meterpreter port. If you started the handler this is you - if you did not, something is calling home.
Second-choice Metasploit handler port. Same reasoning as 4444.
SaltStack publish port. Unauthenticated exposure has led to mass compromise (CVE-2020-11651).
SaltStack return port. See 4505.
Cisco Smart Install. Unauthenticated configuration download and overwrite.
UPnP on some devices, Flask/Docker-registry/AirPlay on others. Identify the process before trusting it.
Common secondary dev-server port; also iperf.
SIP VoIP signalling. Scanned constantly for toll fraud.
SIP over TLS.
mDNS/Bonjour (avahi). Normal on a desktop; it does advertise your hostname and services on the LAN.
PostgreSQL. Normal on loopback (Metasploit's msfdb uses it); should not face the network.
Android Debug Bridge over TCP. Unauthenticated shell on the device; also used by worms.
Kibana web UI. Usually unauthenticated in the free tier.
RabbitMQ/AMQP broker. Default guest:guest credentials are common.
VNC over HTTP (Java viewer). Legacy and usually unauthenticated.
VNC remote desktop. Password is capped at 8 characters and often absent entirely.
VNC display :1. Same reasoning as 5900.
TeamViewer. Remote control software; a legitimate install or an unwanted one.
CouchDB HTTP API. Admin-party mode leaves it wide open.
Windows Remote Management (HTTP). Remote PowerShell; a primary lateral-movement route.
Windows Remote Management (HTTPS).
X11 display :0. With access control off, anyone can read your keystrokes and screen.
X11 display :1. See 6000.
Redis. No authentication by default; exposed it is a well-known path to writing SSH keys or cron jobs as the redis user.
Kubernetes API server. Cluster-wide control plane.
Alternate IRC port. Historically the classic botnet C2 channel.
IRC. Legitimate chat, and the original malware C2 protocol - check what is connected.
IRC over TLS.
Oracle WebLogic. A long list of unauthenticated deserialisation RCEs.
Alternate HTTP. python -m http.server lives here; fine on loopback, an unintended file share when exposed.
Tomcat AJP connector. Ghostcat (CVE-2020-1938) reads and can execute application files.
HTTP proxy / alternate web port. Burp Suite's default listener. On loopback that is expected; exposed, anyone on the network can proxy through you and read your intercepted traffic.
Secondary web/proxy port (Nexus, Jenkins agents, dev servers).
Hadoop YARN ResourceManager. Unauthenticated job submission is remote code execution.
Alternate HTTPS, usually an admin console (Tomcat, VMware, appliances).
Nessus scanner web UI.
Jupyter, alternate proxies and dev servers. A Jupyter notebook without a token is remote code execution.
php-fpm, SonarQube, MinIO and portainer all default here. FastCGI exposed is remote code execution.
supervisord XML-RPC, also Tor's control port on some setups.
Cassandra CQL. Default install has authentication disabled.
Tor SOCKS proxy. Expected if you run Tor; exposed it is an open anonymising relay for others.
Tor control port. Whoever reaches it controls your Tor client, including where traffic goes.
Cockpit web console (root-level host management) or Prometheus.
Kafka broker. Usually unauthenticated inside a trust boundary.
Raw printing (JetDirect). Accepts arbitrary PostScript/PJL; also Prometheus node_exporter on some hosts.
Elasticsearch HTTP API. Unauthenticated by default in older versions - full data read and write.
Elasticsearch cluster transport. Joining the cluster is enough to read everything.
No standard service. Common for hand-rolled listeners and CTF challenges.
Webmin. Root-level host administration over the web; several unauthenticated RCEs.
Memcached. No authentication, and the single worst UDP amplification reflector on the internet.
MongoDB. Historically bound to 0.0.0.0 with no authentication; the reason for a decade of data leaks.
MongoDB shard server.
Back Orifice and about a thousand imitators. Not a real service.
NetBus backdoor's default port, and a favourite of hand-placed listeners.
NetBus secondary port.
SubSeven backdoor default port.
SAP, DB2 and a lot of ad-hoc listeners. Identify the process.
No legitimate service. Common backdoor/CTF port.
